::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Read [Use a structure as a subunit](nested-structures.qmd) first.
Every construction below
uses explicit `Add` and `Link` calls.
:::

**A complete structure can be used as a subunit in a larger structure.**
First build a star with a ring core and six rod arms. Then use that complete
star three times to make a chain, then connect three copies of that chain.
Every copy keeps all of its internal subunits and links.

All components live in the same `World`. Lengths are in nm and q in nm⁻¹.

## 1. Build a ring with six rod arms

Each rod attaches by one endpoint to the ring contour. The six different
`#` labels select independent attachment locations on that contour:

```{python}
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("RingStarChain")
star = world.Add("ThinCircle", "ring")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod1.end1", "ring.contour#arm1", "rod")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod2.end1", "ring.contour#arm2", "rod")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod3.end1", "ring.contour#arm3", "rod")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod4.end1", "ring.contour#arm4", "rod")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod5.end1", "ring.contour#arm5", "rod")
world.Link("ThinRod", "rod6.end1", "ring.contour#arm6", "rod")
world.Add(star, "star")

parameters = {
    "R_ring": 4.0,
    "beta_ring": 1.0,
    "L_rod": 10.0,
    "beta_rod": 1.0,
}

view_options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Nanometer)
view_options.seed = 7
view_options.layout_mode = pyseb.LayoutMode.Readable

star_view = pyseb.visualize(world, "star", parameters, view_options, height=460)
```

The tag `"rod"` makes all six rods share `L_rod` and `beta_rod`. The names
`rod1` through `rod6` still identify the individual arms.

The ring is rigid, and each arm is a rigid rod with a freely jointed
attachment. The contour references are distributed: the model averages over
attachment positions, rather than fixing six equally spaced points. The view
shows one representative arrangement.

`star` is the graph of the whole connected structure. We can pass that graph
to `Add` and `Link`, just as we previously passed a primitive type.

## 2. Chain three complete stars together

Connect the free endpoint of one star's `rod2` to the free endpoint of the
next star's `rod1`:

```{python}
chain = world.Add(star, "star1")
world.Link(star, "star2:rod1.end2", "star1:rod2.end2")
world.Link(star, "star3:rod1.end2", "star2:rod2.end2")
world.Add(chain, "chain")

chain_view = pyseb.visualize(world, "chain", parameters, view_options, height=600)
```

Each `Link` adds a **complete six-arm star**. The chain contains three rings
and eighteen rods. We wrote the construction of the star only once.

Two arms form each connection between neighbouring ring cores. The remaining
arms have free endpoints. These links allow the stars to rotate relative to
one another; they do not prescribe a straight chain.

## 3. Connect three complete chains

Now reuse `chain` itself. Join the last star in one chain to the first star
in the next chain, using the arms that are still free:

```{python}
chain_of_chains = world.Add(chain, "chain1")
world.Link(chain, "chain2:star1:rod1.end2", "chain1:star3:rod2.end2")
world.Link(chain, "chain3:star1:rod1.end2", "chain2:star3:rod2.end2")
world.Add(chain_of_chains, "chainOfChains")

chains_view = pyseb.visualize(
    world, "chainOfChains", parameters, view_options, height=650
)
```

This is **chain1 – chain2 – chain3**. Each chain contains three stars, so the
complete structure contains nine rings and fifty-four rods. Each `Link`
adds a whole chain; it keeps the star-to-star connections made above.

The resulting connectivity is a chain of nine stars. Grouping them into
three reusable chains introduces another hierarchy level without adding
extra scattering material at the group boundaries.

## 4. Read references through two hierarchy levels

A colon moves inside an instance. In `chain2:star1:rod1.end2`, we go
through two named structures before reaching the rod:

| Part of the path | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `chain2` | Which instance of the complete chain |
| `star1` | Which star inside that chain |
| `rod1` | Which arm inside that star |
| `end2` | The free endpoint of that rod |

Compare the paths as the structure gets deeper:

```text
rod1.end2                  endpoint in one star
star1:rod1.end2            endpoint in a chain of stars
chain2:star1:rod1.end2     endpoint in a chain of chains
```

## 5. Change one parameter in every copy

**All nine stars share the same parameters.** The instance paths identify
individual rods and rings, but do not create new parameter names:

| Parameter | What changes in the complete structure |
| --- | --- |
| `L_rod` | Length of all 54 rods |
| `beta_rod` | Scattering weight of each of the 54 rods |
| `R_ring` | Radius of all nine rings |
| `beta_ring` | Scattering weight of each of the nine rings |

To see this, set the shared rod length to 0.1 nm in a copy of the parameter
dictionary and display the same structure again:

```{python}
short_rods = dict(parameters, L_rod=0.1)

rings_view = pyseb.visualize(
    world, "chainOfChains", short_rods, view_options, height=650
)
```

Every arm becomes short at once, so neighbouring rings nearly meet at their
linked contour locations. The graph still contains the same nine rings and 54 rods;
we changed one parameter without rebuilding any of the stars or chains.
The rings are connected by short rods; they are not physically interlocked.

The small positive length also works for scattering calculations. Shortening
rods does not remove their scattering: `beta_rod` is still 1 for every rod.
Set `beta_rod=0` if you want only the rings to contribute to scattering;
the rod length still controls the spacing between rings.

The original `parameters` dictionary still has `L_rod=10`, which we use for
the scattering curves below.

## 6. Calculate the scattering of each structure

Evaluate each complete structure by its public name:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

q = np.geomspace(0.001, 2.0, 180)
star_curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("star", parameters, q.tolist())
chain_curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("chain", parameters, q.tolist())
chains_curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("chainOfChains", parameters, q.tolist())

plt.loglog(q, star_curve, label="One six-arm star")
plt.loglog(q, chain_curve, label="Chain of three stars")
plt.loglog(q, chains_curve, label="Three chains: nine stars")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ [nm$^{-1}$]")
plt.ylabel("Normalized form factor F(q)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

These are normalized curves: all approach one at low q, despite their
different total scattering lengths. Each calculation includes the
scattering from all rings and rods, including interference between its stars.
The internal subunits remain part of the calculation.

The viewers use seeded, readability-optimized orientations. Scattering
averages over the orientations allowed by the freely jointed links and the
distributed attachment locations; displayed overlaps do not introduce
excluded-volume interactions.
